data.translation:
T3 Code project’s dirty laundry, installment ⑱:

It took T3 Code more than 8 months to reach 30,000 stars, but in the past 20-plus days it shot up to 77,000 stars. Yet the repo has only 129 watchers.

Where did those extra 40,000-plus stars come from?

Back at the end of April, Theo made a dedicated 36-minute video about fake GitHub stars, writing in the caption that GitHub stars had long since stopped reflecting genuine popularity and had mostly become a tool companies use to fool VCs into investing.

By the end of October, T3 Code was stuck at around 30,000 stars. In a tweet, he mentioned seeing people question the project’s popularity based on its GitHub star count.

On October 30, Theo opened and merged PR #27832 himself, adding a pop-up in the top-right corner of the client: once a user had sent 5 prompts, it would pop up asking for a star. Before showing the pop-up, it would first call the local GitHub API to check whether that account had already starred the repo.

On November 2, he posted a tweet with a graph of star growth. After the dashed line marked “Star prompt,” the previously flat line shot almost straight up.

In the caption, he said that after adding this prompt, the number of new stars per day immediately increased tenfold. A few hours later, he posted a screenshot of the GitHub Trending list, pointing with a red arrow at T3 Code’s 3,094 new stars that day, saying the trick worked way too well.

On November 3, a user commented that they would just close the pop-up while working, but would click it if they were idle.

Just over an hour later, Theo opened and merged PRs #29922 and #29987 himself, taking this star-solicitation mechanism up another notch.

First, it was changed to wait until the window had been idle for 30 seconds before popping up, specifically targeting the moments when users are staring blankly while waiting for the agent to work.

Second, clicking the button no longer redirected to the GitHub website. Instead, it went through the newly added https://t.co/r8037jbYm7 endpoint, with the backend directly using the GitHub credentials logged in on the server machine to send a PUT user/starred/pingdotgg/t3code request and star the repo, then set off a round of confetti in the UI.

When PR #29922 was opened, the repo’s built-in review bot, Macroscope, flagged it as requiring human approval because the star was being added using the server’s GitHub account, which was not necessarily the same person as the user who clicked the button.

Theo didn’t wait for anyone else to approve it. He merged the code into the main branch himself.

On November 6, developer zhilsinger left a review comment on PR #29922, demanding that the server-side starring on the user’s behalf be removed and that it go back to opening the user’s own browser.

He listed two specific problems.

First, on a remote or shared server, the server doesn’t know who clicked the button. It directly uses the GitHub credentials on that machine to star the repo on someone else’s behalf, and the pop-up never shows which account was actually used. Even the source code’s own comments admit that on a shared server, this account may not belong to the current user.

Second, looking at the code in packages/source-control-github/src/server/driver.ts, starredPath only checks that the path has two segments and contains no dots. The server never locks the target repo to pingdotgg/t3code, so any client with source-control:write permission can use the server’s credentials to star any repo.

This review comment sat there for 19 days with no reply, and the code was never changed.

Using this flow—triggered after sending 5 prompts, waiting 30 seconds of inactivity for the pop-up, then using local credentials to call the API and star the repo directly—T3 Code went from 30,000 stars to 77,000 stars in 25 days.

On November 7, Theo also tweeted asking his followers to help push it to 50,000 stars. By November 24, he posted a screenshot showing 74,600 stars, saying he had somehow completely failed to notice when it broke 70,000 stars a few days earlier.

That’s basically the whole story behind this project’s 70,000-plus stars.

November 2 post showing the vertical spike and admitting daily new stars had increased tenfold: https://t.co/PPG40IpoQF
November 2 post showing +3,094 stars in a single day and a rise to the top of GitHub Trending: https://t.co/cG6DGeaPMm
November 24 post saying he completely failed to notice it breaking 70,000 stars: https://t.co/lHlBIUYK06
